summary: Abi Aryan delivers a comprehensive presentation on domain adaptation and fine-tuning for large language models, aimed at helping practitioners make informed decisions for enterprise or hobby use cases. She frames the problem around three motivations: LLMs like ChatGPT and open-source models are not trained for every domain, with some under-represented due to compliance or data scarcity; collecting new data for each domain is costly; and personalization demands broad accessibility. She notes that modern embedding-based learning enables cross-language transfer because semantically similar languages share structure. Aryan reviews transformer model architecture—encoder, decoder, feed-forward and attention networks—and explains fine-tuning as updating parameters (weights and biases) to improve pre-trained model performance. She distinguishes updating all weights (transfer learning, cross-distillation—expensive and storage-heavy) versus partial updates including instruction tuning, RLHF (impractical due to human labeling cost), and three parameter-efficient techniques. Adapter tuning adds small parameter components achieving performance matching with only 0.15% of parameters, suited for new domains like biochemical engineering. Prefix tuning introduces prefixes that mimic behavior via an embedding layer at the front of the attention layer. LoRA identifies linearly independent layers in weight matrices to reduce size for resource-constrained devices; QLoRA quantizes to 4-bit precision but requires specific libraries and lacks comprehensive testing, so she recommends LoRA. She then compares prompting (good for generalizable models and demos, requires less data, cheaper but less performant), RAGs, and fine-tuning. Fine-tuning itself divides into three approaches: adaptive fine-tuning (optimizing for an entire target domain with multiple tasks, e.g., legal), behavioral fine-tuning (optimizing for a single target task, analogous to LangChain function calls, helpful for inference and reasoning), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (standard approach freezing most parameters). These techniques can be combined with prompt engineering and RAGs. She stresses that success depends on data quality—collection, tokenization, cleaning, normalization, noise removal, deduplication (which reduces memorization and bias), and augmentation. For optimization, she advises against comparing fine-tuned models to GPT-4/5, recommends in-context learning with dynamic examples for data drift, breaking tasks into smaller sub-tasks, and implementing gradient checkpointing to reduce memory usage despite higher computation. On hyperparameters, she suggests batch size 32 or 64, 100 epochs as a starting point for domain optimization (one for quick tests), Adam optimizer, and early stopping for regularization. For evaluation, she identifies four components: metric-based (BLEU, ROUGE), tool-based (Weights & Biases AutoEvaluate), model-based (using a smaller model to evaluate, with potential for standardization and automation), and human-in-the-loop (common but inefficient). She concludes that fine-tuning requires thinking about the entire pipeline—data collection, storage management, base model selection, and risk management—for robust, production-grade applications.

sections.title: Introduction & Motivation for Domain Adaptation
sections.summary: Aryan introduces the talk as an overview of domain adaptation and fine-tuning. She outlines three reasons to care: LLMs are not trained for every domain, collecting new data is costly, and personalization requires broad accessibility. She notes embedding-based learning enables cross-language transfer for semantically similar languages.

sections.title: Fine-tuning Fundamentals & Transformer Architecture
sections.summary: Reviews transformer model structure—encoder, decoder, feed-forward and attention networks storing weights and biases. Defines fine-tuning as teaching models to learn tasks they were not originally trained for by updating parameters.

sections.title: Weight Update Methods Overview
sections.summary: Distinguishes updating all weights (transfer learning, cross-distillation—expensive, more storage) versus updating some weights. Lists adapter tuning, prefix tuning, parameter-efficient tuning, instruction tuning, and RLHF. Notes RLHF is impractical due to human labeling cost, leaving three main techniques.

sections.title: Adapter-based Tuning
sections.summary: Explains adapter tuning adds small parameter components to the existing transformer model. Achieves performance matching with only 0.15% of parameters. Best suited for learning entirely new domains like biochemical engineering.

sections.title: Prefix-based Tuning
sections.summary: Describes prefix tuning as introducing prefixes that store model weights and mimic behavior by adding an embedding layer at the front of the attention layer. Uses a water tank and tap analogy to explain how output takes form without changing underlying model behavior.

sections.title: Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning: LoRA and QLoRA
sections.summary: Covers LoRA (low-rank adaptation) which identifies linearly independent layers in weight matrices to reduce size, ideal for running large models on constrained devices. QLoRA quantizes weights to 4-bit precision but requires specific libraries and lacks comprehensive testing. Recommends LoRA over QLoRA currently.

sections.title: Domain Adaptation Methods Comparison
sections.summary: Compares prompting (good for generalizable models and demos, less data, cheaper but less performant—about 10 examples is good per ChatGPT), RAGs, and fine-tuning. Fine-tuning divides into adaptive (optimizing for entire target domain with multiple tasks, e.g., legal), behavioral (optimizing for single target task, analogous to LangChain function calls, helpful for inference/reasoning), and parameter-efficient (standard approach freezing most parameters). These can be combined with prompt engineering and RAGs.

sections.title: Data Quality Considerations
sections.summary: Emphasizes that fine-tuning success depends on data quality: collection, tokenization, cleaning, normalization, noise removal, and sanitization. Highlights data deduplication—research shows model memorization is mainly caused by duplicate entries, and removing them reduces bias and memorization. Also covers data augmentation.

sections.title: Model Optimization Best Practices
sections.summary: Advises against comparing fine-tuned models to GPT-4/5 for complex tasks. Recommends in-context learning with dynamic example loading to handle data drift and manage costs. Suggests breaking tasks into smaller sub-tasks rather than training for an entire language. Recommends gradient checkpointing to reduce memory consumption despite higher recomputation during backward pass.

sections.title: Hyperparameters & Regularization
sections.summary: Covers hyperparameter selection: batch size 32 or 64, 100 epochs as starting point for domain optimization (one for quick Google Colab tests), Adam optimizer as standard general-purpose choice. Recommends early stopping for regularization, noting many current models are not squeezing optimal performance. Advises reconsidering batch and embeddings if performance declines.

sections.title: Model Evaluation Framework
sections.summary: Explains evaluation as the hardest part, noting log accuracy and perplexity alone are insufficient. Proposes four evaluation components: metric-based (BLEU, ROUGE), tool-based (Weights & Biases AutoEvaluate for compilation errors), model-based (smaller model evaluates another—hard but has potential for standardization and automation), and human-in-the-loop (common but inefficient).

sections.title: Pipeline Considerations & Conclusion
sections.summary: Concludes that fine-tuning requires thinking about the entire pipeline—data collection, storage management, base model selection—for robust production applications. Emphasizes catching issues early to avoid reputational and compliance risks, managing data drift and prompt drift, and treating fine-tuning as a big-picture decision for sustained performance.
